quote: Welches sind die notwendigen der Anschauung entnommenen Postulate, auf Grund deren später alles nur Logik (Schematismus) wird.
english: Which are the necessary postulates taken from intuition, on the basis of which everything afterwards becomes mere logic (schematism)?
topic: Hilbert notes lecture plans (reading elliptic functions following Liouville, and a course on pure geometry with axioms, Euclidean geometry, analysis situs and projective geometry), a plan to study when two solutions of his discriminant problem coincide, and a remark that an irrational number contains nothing infinite.

triage.modern_statement: Find a minimal, complete set of basic axioms for geometry, the ones that come from spatial intuition, from which every geometric theorem then follows by pure logical deduction (a formal 'schematism'), with no further appeal to intuition. In modern terms this is the program of axiomatizing elementary geometry. It includes showing that the axioms are complete, consistent and independent of each other. This is a foundational, programmatic question rather than a single theorem.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert himself. He worked on it in his geometry lectures of 1891–1899 (starting with the 1891 projective geometry course in Königsberg) and answered it in 'Grundlagen der Geometrie' (1899). That book sets out five groups of axioms (incidence, order, congruence, parallels, continuity) and studies how consistent and independent they are. The same idea was then extended to physics as the 6th of his 1900 problems. Logic-based (Tarski-style) axiomatizations of elementary geometry came later; the searches I ran did not cover those.

evidence.claim: In the introduction to Grundlagen der Geometrie, Hilbert says geometry needs only a few simple principles (the axioms) to be built up logically. He says choosing these axioms and studying how they relate 'is tantamount to the logical analysis of our intuition of space.'

Hilbert sorts the axioms into five groups. He says each group expresses 'certain related fundamental facts of our intuition.' In other words, the axioms are postulates taken from intuition, which is exactly what the diary note asks for.

Hilbert's lectures on the foundations of geometry from 1891 to 1902 are documented in Hallett & Majer (2004). His first geometry lecture was on projective geometry, and his foundational work was shaped by earlier axiomatic projective geometry.
In the Grundlagen, Hilbert links the axioms explicitly to basic facts of intuition. Scholars discuss how his axiomatic method later separated the formal system from spatial intuition.
Hilbert's 6th problem (1900), the axiomatization of physics, grew out of his own research on the foundations of geometry.

triage.why: The page plans a pure-geometry course with axioms, Euclidean geometry, analysis situs and projective geometry. Read in that context, the note asks which intuition-based axioms make the rest of geometry purely logical. That is the program Hilbert carried out in his 1891–1899 lectures and in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), whose introduction says almost the same thing. So, read this way, the question was answered, by Hilbert himself, rather than staying open. The axiomatization of geometry is also no longer an active open research question. Confidence is medium, not high, for three reasons. The note is short and philosophical. It might refer to analysis situs or arithmetic rather than Euclidean geometry. And the question of what intuition contributes is still debated philosophically, though not as an open mathematical problem.
